newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka leader's India visit fuels peace rumours.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka leader's India visit fuels peace rumours.

text.p: Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga's sudden visit to India this week has raised speculation of renewed peace talks with Tamil Tiger separatist guerrillas, analysts said on Thursday.

"India could probably play the role of a facilitator in peace talks," former air force chief air vice marshal Harry Goonetileke told Reuters. "I always believed there is an India factor in our ethnic problem. I feel some discreet discussions are on the cards."

Kumaratunga arrived in India with her two children on Tuesday on what was officially described as a holiday but she is scheduled to hold talks with Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda at the end of her visit.

Her trip coincides with reports of impending talks with Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, who are fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the Indian Ocean island's north and east.
But Indian and Sri Lankan officials have played down reports of a link between Kumaratunga's visit and rumoured peace initiatives with the Tigers.

India has been closely involved in Sri Lanka's turbulent ethnic crises, providing armed assistance to Colombo in fending off a hardline Sinhalese-led rebellion and by sending in troops in a failed attempt in 1987 to disarm the LTTE.
Goonetileke said he felt India was unlikely to get involved militarily again except by providing more training to Sri Lankan security forces and sharing intelligence on rebel activities.
"India is likely to take up with Kumaratunga the issue of some 250,000 Tamils displaced by the latest fighting," he said.
Some other analysts contacted by Reuters declined to comment on Kumaratunga's visit.

Sri Lankan newspapers have reported the presence in the island of Kumar Rupasinghe of the International Alert conflict resolution outfit, saying he could be a go-between in the efforts to revive peace talks.
Rupasinghe is expected to meet LTTE leaders in northeastern Mullaitivu, where the rebels have their main jungle bases, political analysts said.
Rupasinghe could not be reached immediately for comment.
LTTE sources have said Kumaratunga's government had encouraged a peace initiative recently by an international humanitarian group but they gave no details.
They said any progress towards peace with the LTTE would hinge on the government's attitude to Tiger chieftain Velupillai Prabhakaran's latest peace offer in November.
Prabhakaran has demanded the withdrawal of Sri Lankan troops from Tamil areas in the north as one of the conditions for resuming talks with Colombo, they said.

The government has said it will only resume talks with the Tigers if they make a substantial surrender of arms and agree to a fixed time table for negotiations to end the 13-year war in which it says more than 50,000 people have been killed.
The Tigers torpedoed the last round of peace talks in April last year by sinking two navy gunboats in the eastern port of Trincomalee in an underwater suicide attack.
Both sides have dealt each other heavy blows in the bitter fighting since then but neither side has managed to tilt the military balance.

Kumaratunga last year unveiled a peace plan offering extensive autonomy to Tamils as an alternative to a separate state but it has been stalled in parliament because of bickering with the opposition United National Party.
